stories.title: How Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI technology
stories.summary: Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI. Its security team investigates threats faster and proposes patches in minutes.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: How Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI technology
sources.text: Block is using AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak to compress the time to fix vulnerabilities, freeing its security team to focus on strategic work. Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry Minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch Analyst-hours of investigation completed each quarter At Block, the company behind Square, Cash App, and Afterpay, the security team leverages the OpenAI Defense Factory: where AI handles vulnerability discovery, detection, and response at a scale that no human team could keep up with. With AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak, Block is taking just hours to do work that used to take weeks. Block’s security team has been focused on responsibly adopting AI across workflows, whether that’s code generation or security operations. “What it’s really centered on is having a new teammate that you can scale with,” James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, says. “It’s not like a more traditional automation where you had to go step by step. You can prompt it with a fairly bespoke, ambiguous problem and work through it together.” Projects like reviewing a software bug or parsing a log would take days or weeks to complete. Now the team can complete those projects in a fraction of the time, with a human still validating every result. For example, for detection tuning, every investigation stores its raw query evidence, so the team can now replay a proposed detection change against seven months of production telemetry in under an hour. That work used to mean requerying hundreds of old cases by hand, and often it rarely happened in practice since it was so time-consuming. The team has also gotten more particular about which model they’re using for which job. “We used to use the latest model, but you don’t need to do that anymore,” he says. “It’s been a learning experience to choose different models for different tasks.” Block’s security harness is built on top of Daybreak to help route tasks to the right model, and it includes hooks for humans to take over tasks or for agents to verify each other’s work. The team continually evaluates these systems against internal benchmarks and real-world performance, adjusting its approach when needed, including routing work to human review when that is the responsible path. The automated triage system has resulted in faster work (and more of it) getting done. Block’s security team has seen a 50% boost to triage throughput, a 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations, and an entirely new autonomous hunting capability. Nettesheim says, “This performs ~1,100 analyst-hours of investigation per quarter, because every alert now gets a full, deep investigation across all elements the alert involves. Our system works every alert like it’s the only alert we’ve got that day.” Traditional scanning tools flag a single vulnerability in isolation, but Block’s security team can go much further with Daybreak. The model helps hypothesize about attack patterns and chain together a series of attacks into a full end-to-end compromise path, surfacing vulnerabilities that might have existed for years. In one case, an alert on a single laptop looked like a minor policy issue on its own. But during peer review, the model followed an indicator that appeared only incidentally in the evidence, joined it against Block’s identity logs, and surfaced a much larger set of issues. “One routine endpoint alert became a campaign takedown. No single tool makes that join. The signal only exists across two products’ logs,” James says. Another example when Daybreak helped was during a recent red team exercise. The model was given a few hints about an internal system, and it chained together a full attack path—SQL injection, privilege escalation, a foothold, credential enumeration, and a pivot to other systems—in about two hours. This would typically take a human red teamer several days. In recent red team exercises, the time from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch was 18 minutes. Finding the vulnerabilities is only as good as the ability to fix them. Nettesheim walks through the process his team uses on every finding: locate where the issue lives in the code and identify who owns it, then move to remediation. “You propose a patch, you confirm exploitability, and then you verify that you have fixed it, with a human in the loop guiding it and deploying the code changes.” While agents are technically capable, they don’t carry an organization’s context or the reasoning behind previous decisions. A human provides that context and strategy, and that’s where his team comes in to provide a human layer of review. As AI’s judgment is proven out in practice, Nettesheim says, “we’ll slowly ladder up the risk level to use it for more sensitive systems.” Less than one hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry. 18 minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch in recent red team exercises. Roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter of false-positive triage handed back. Approximately 1,100 analyst-hours of investigation completed per quarter. 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations. Detection and response work alone has handed back roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter that used to go toward triaging false positives. With that time back, the team now spends more time on deeper investigations and building more automation responsibly. As the pace of attack increases and AI models keep advancing, Nettesheim sees an opportunity to reduce the number of vulnerabilities introduced in the first place. That would free security teams to spend less time patching and more time on preventative, strategic work. “OpenAI is shifting the advantage to defenders by putting these advanced capabilities in everyone’s hands,” he says. “It’s typically only been in very high-profile technology compan

sources.title: How Tamnoon built AI-powered cloud security remediation with Amazon Bedrock
sources.text: Critical cloud exposures pile up faster than security teams can close them. Cloud-native application protection platforms (CNAPP), cloud providers, and posture scanners generate more findings than any team can triage, and risk accumulates in the gap between detected and fixed. Most findings sit untouched, not because they’re hard to fix. Someone must investigate context, identify the owner, confirm the fix won’t break production, and then do it at a volume that outpaces headcount. In this post, we share how Tamnoon built Tami, an agentic cloud remediation orchestrator on Amazon Bedrock , to close that gap. Tami autonomously investigates findings ingested from CNAPP and cloud-native sources and assesses whether remediation is safe. It then generates and orchestrates the fix with guardrails and governance wherever a change touches a customer’s cloud. The approach drove an over 90 percent reduction in critical cloud exposure in 90 days with zero production issues. Tamnoon is an AI-powered cloud security remediation platform that works alongside CNAPPs. Its AI assistant, Tami, helps human cloud security experts investigate, prioritize, and safely remediate misconfigurations and issues across customer environments in AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, and other cloud providers. Tamnoon integrates with the CNAPPs and cloud-native tools teams already use and turns their findings into validated, production-safe fixes. Most of the work including investigation, prioritization, and remediation planning happens before anything touches a live environment, which is what makes automated remediation trustworthy at scale. A security engineer can spend hours investigating a single finding. Often, it traces back to the same root cause as dozens of other alerts. Tamnoon’s solution addresses the full pipeline from finding ingestion to validated fix. The platform treats these challenges as interconnected rather than isolated problems. Tamnoon takes you from initial finding to executing the fix. The platform ingests findings from CNAPP, Cloud Security Posture Management (CSPM) providers, and other security tools and normalizes them into a unified schema. It then enriches them with asset and exposure context and prioritizes them. From there, the agentic layer takes over using a set of specialized AI agents, each running in an event-driven, serverless architecture on AWS, so every stage scales independently and fails safely. The platform delegates work to four specialized agents, each responsible for a distinct phase of the remediation pipeline: When the Tamnoon team set out to build Tami, the choice of foundation model (FM) platform was going to shape everything that followed. Tamnoon’s remediation agents don’t all do the same kind of work. Some perform deep investigative reasoning to understand the root cause of a security finding. Others handle high-volume validation, checking proposed fixes quickly and cheaply. Still others review generated code, balancing quality against cost on every task. Matching each of these jobs to the right model, without stitching together a different integration for each one, was a core requirement. That requirement is what made Amazon Bedrock the natural fit. Through a single API, each agent can call the foundation model best suited to its task. The most capable models handle the hardest reasoning. More efficient models take on the repetitive, high-throughput work. Review-focused models optimize the trade-off between output quality and cost. Because it’s one integration rather than many, models can be swapped or upgraded as the landscape evolves, without re-plumbing the architecture each time. Operational overhead at scale was another factor in the decision. As request volume grew, Tamnoon wanted to avoid building and maintaining its own logic to distribute traffic across regional capacity. Amazon Bedrock Cross-Region inference handles this automatically. It automatically routes inference requests to the optimal AWS Region within a defined geographic boundary, maintaining throughput without requiring any custom routing code to operate. Security was the final consideration, and for a cloud security company it was non-negotiable. With Bedrock, inference runs inside Tamnoon’s own AWS environment under AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM)-scoped permissions. Sensitive customer data never leaves the trust boundary. That gave the team confidence that the platform underpinning Tami met the same standard Tamnoon holds its own service to. Tamnoon sits downstream of the detection tools security teams already run. CNAPPs like Wiz, CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Cortex, Upwind, SentinelOne, Orca, and Cyera along with cloud-native services like AWS Security Hub and Amazon GuardDuty are the source of truth for what’s wrong in the environment. Tamnoon connects through API-based integrations and normalizes findings into a common format, so a misconfiguration looks the same whether it came from Wiz or GuardDuty. The detection tools remain the foundation. Tamnoon delivers the end-to-end remediation that follows. For every finding it works, Tami assigns a Remediation Confidence Indicator (RCI) of SAFE, RISKY, or AWAITING DATA. That rating tells teams what can be automated and what needs human review first. Tamnoon runs entirely within its own AWS accounts, isolated per environment. Users access the platform through a single secure entry point built on Amazon API Gateway, with encryption managed by AWS Certificate Manager and sign-in handled by Amazon Cognito. Everything behind that entry point runs in private networks across multiple Availability Zones, so the core platform is never directly exposed to the internet. Inside that environment, Tamnoon combines two kinds of compute. Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) runs the always-on services behind the dashboard, while AWS Lambda powers the event-driven work of collecting findings, analyzing them, and executing remediations. sources.title: What it takes to trust AI with real-world fixes
sources.text: We designed a layered model that lets an AI agent resolve production network incidents on its own within defined identity, authorization, tooling, and human-approval boundaries. It’s 2:00 am. A pager goes off. A link somewhere in a datacenter has started flapping, a handful of alarms have correlated into one incident, and the on-call engineer is now doing what on-call engineers have always done: opening five tabs, one per system, and reconstructing what happened from fragments. We built an AI agent to do that reconstruction. It works. It pulls the device state, reads the telemetry, correlates the recent changes, classifies the failure, and writes a clean summary into the incident before the human has finished logging in. It also knows the fix. And that is where the demo stops being a demo. Because the agent “knows the fix,” the question is whether the system should allow it to shut a BGP session on a device that’s carrying live customer traffic. A “read” is something you can double-check. A “write” is an action that already happened. The moment an agent can change production, every property you were relaxed about at the read stage becomes a potential source of customer impact and risk. This post is about what we learned building an agent that’s trusted to take that action, as well as the uncomfortable conclusion we kept arriving at: There is no single thing you can build that makes an agent safe to run in production. Not a smarter model, not a stricter prompt, not a clever guardrail. Safe autonomy requires a stack. Ask 10 builders for a definition, and you’ll get 10 answers—and most of them are really examples (“You know, like a coding agent”) rather than definitions. That’s fine; we’re still in the relatively early days of agentic AI. But the fuzziness hides what matters here. An agent is not the model. The model is the brilliant, non-deterministic part in the middle. The agent is the deterministic software wrapped around it—the part that decides what the model is asked, what it may do with the answer, which tools it can reach, and what happens when it is wrong. The model supplies intelligence. The agent supplies judgment about how far to trust that intelligence and what to let it touch. Seen that way, the interesting engineering in an agentic system is usually the wrapper. And the whole safety question reframes with that distinction: Making an agent safe is less about a smarter model in the middle and more about a better deterministic shell around it. Concretely, the harness we wrap around the model during execution is a mostly-deterministic workflow with a few narrow, schema-checked model steps inside it. It is what turns “the model worked something out once” into “these steps run the same way every time.” You don’t need its full mechanics yet—that’s another layer. For now, just hold the picture: a deterministic workflow with the model kept on a short leash inside it. Harness, agent, orchestrator, playbook, call it what you like. The load-bearing idea is the same: deterministic software putting a non-deterministic model to work, on purpose, within limits. The “holy grail” of agentic development is an agent that can investigate a problem, work out a fix, and carry it out without a human directing every step. But getting there in production means building safety into each step. More autonomy should not mean fewer controls. Imagine giving that agent a service account with broad access, a shell that can run anything, and a stern system prompt listing everything it must never do. It might have everything it needs to fix the problem. But what actually prevents it from taking an action it shouldn’t take? A broadly privileged service account can give the agent more access than the person who invoked it. An unrestricted shell can put anything that account and machine can reach within the impact radius. A system prompt helps guide behavior, but it can’t enforce permissions. The model can misinterpret an instruction or be influenced by malicious text in a log or tool response. Production safety can’t depend on instructions to the model alone. The hard part of autonomy is authorization, not intelligence. Modern models are frighteningly good at figuring out the fix. The real question is: “What is this thing allowed to do, under whose identity, through what interface, and with whose sign off?” It’s boring, it’s deterministic, and it’s the whole game. Once we started stacking boundaries, the architecture fell into four layers. Each answers a different question. None of them are sufficient alone, and that’s the point. Read bottom to top, it’s defense in depth across identity, tool, mutation, and time. Read as a sentence: The agent acts only as the human who summoned it (identity), reaches production only through a controlled interface (tool), can read freely but must pause before it changes anything (mutation), and gets less reliant on live reasoning the more it runs (time). Two of these are security controls in the literal sense: identity and tool access are where an attacker or a hallucination does its damage, so that’s where the hardest walls go. The agent doesn’t get its own powerful account. It acts on behalf of the human who invoked it, bounded by that person’s real permissions. Where a service identity is unavoidable, it gets the narrower of the two. Identity is compound: the human plus the agent, and the stricter one wins. Access policies are owned by the teams that own each tool, defined per tool, and changed through a normal pull request (PR) with the tool team as a required reviewer. Merging a PR grants access; reverting it revokes access. The agent never gets a bare shell. Every capability it has sits behind a single typed tool interface, each tool is individually authorized, and each call is structured and logged. Note the careful wording: The enemy is not the command line; it is the unbounded one. A raw shell cannot be governed, because you cannot put a permission boundary, a schema, or

stories.title: Developing Gemini 4 Argon responsibly and safely

sources.name: Google DeepMind
sources.title: Developing Gemini 4 Argon responsibly and safely
sources.text: Learn more about our approach to safety and security for Gemini 4 Argon. Gemini 4 Argon is a step forward in what models can do — especially when it comes to deep work in complex, real-world tasks across domains including coding, finance, legal, cybersecurity, and science. Its cyberdefense capabilities are frontier-level and designed to give defenders an advantage over attackers. To maximize its potential, we first wanted cyber defenders to put it to work via our Fairwind Program , while our own security teams used it to scan critical systems inside and outside of Google. This window of limited access showed why these capabilities matter. For instance, Wiz used Argon to uncover a critical bug in hospital software that previous models had missed, helping protect hundreds of thousands of patient records. Meanwhile, Google’s own security teams used Argon to find and patch bugs across internal software or open-source software. This included fixing foundational vulnerabilities affecting systems globally, which are going through our responsible disclosure process. Today, we are beginning to roll out Argon broadly , as well as expanding our Fairwind Program to additional trusted cyber defenders. To do this well, we grappled with two big questions: Our full Safety and Security Report systematically covers our set of defenses. Below are some highlights from how we approached these two questions for Gemini 4 Argon. The same coding and reasoning improvements that enabled Argon to find and patch vulnerabilities also drove better performance on our cybersecurity tests — solving all 12 of the end-to-end simulated cyberattack scenarios, up from five in our previous generation. In biology evaluations, unguarded versions of the model also showed a much stronger ability to help troubleshoot complex lab procedures step by step. Following our Frontier Safety Framework , since we saw elevated capabilities in the cyber and biological domains, we put our next-generation set of frontier safeguards in place across both areas. First, when it comes to potentially dangerous requests — from writing exploit code to helping with dangerous biological materials, Argon is significantly better at not fulfilling harmful requests than our previous models. On an adversarial set meant to stress test the model, violations reduced nearly twofold — also significantly better than previous Gemini models. Second, we wrap the model in three layers of real-time protection; this is to prevent determined attackers that might try to jailbreak (i.e. trick) the model by disguising a dangerous request as a harmless story or breaking it into dozens of small questions over several weeks. Here is how these protections work: Combining real-time protection, faster fixes for new jailbreaks and enhanced monitoring for recurring misuse has made our systems better at preventing real-world harm. For instance, external bio jailbreak red teaming could only unlock less than 1% of bio sub-tasks we test for. Misalignment can sometimes mean an agent deciding on its own to pursue a goal different to what was intended by the user. Because Argon is much better than earlier models at understanding the environment it is running in, we test carefully for that kind of behavior. For example, we ran realistic "honeypot" tests to see if the model would increase its ability to take covert actions, such as sabotaging safety monitoring. We didn't find any instances of that behavior. But what we do see in practice today is something much more familiar: an agent trying too hard to finish the job it was given. When a resourceful assistant is told to get a task done and runs into a locked door, it can treat that obstacle as just another puzzle to solve. This is why we trained Gemini 4 Argon to respect system boundaries, report negative findings honestly, and pause to ask for human confirmation. On coding benchmarks where models have no incentive to hold back, attempts to take a shortcut or cheat on the task dropped to just 2% on Gemini 4 Argon, our best performance for recent Gemini models. And while this is a major step forward, when a model runs millions of complex tasks, even a rare misstep will eventually show up. As a second line of defense, we built an automated misalignment monitor that reads both the agent’s actions and its internal "scratchpad" (its step-by-step chain of thought) in real time, blocking severe boundary violations before they happen and flagging serious internal cases for human responders. (We continually harden our training and evaluation environments against potential escapes. You can read more about this in our agent control roadmap ). We run this monitor in our products, on our internal coding agents, during our training runs, and during our capability evaluations. When training tasks were difficult or when training environments were flawed, our monitor caught the model, in rare instances, creatively attempting to game the test. The model attempted to escalate container privileges to alter grading scripts, read answers from the test runner's memory, and in one case it even crashed the evaluation sandbox to avoid getting scored for a failed run. While we use these catches to fix flawed tasks, we do not use them to otherwise intervene with the training process to avoid overfitting to the monitor. And we always follow one rule: we don’t penalize the model for what it writes in its chain of thought during training . Here’s an example to illustrate why: in a reinforcement learning training run where a shortcut penalty was accidentally applied to the chain of thought, openly discussed shortcuts dropped by 61%, but that did not mean the model took less shortcuts. Instead, the share of shortcuts the model took silently — without mentioning them in its thoughts — more than tripled (from 11.2% to 36.4%). stories.title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
stories.summary: Learn how the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory and Anchor Browser built AI agents that autonomously pay for x402-protected web resources and APIs. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments checks budgets, signs transactions, and retries requests without exposing wallet credentials to the agent runtime.

sources.name: AWS Machine Learning
sources.title: Building agents that transact with Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments
sources.text: AI agents increasingly need to access web resources that are priced per request. For example, premium datasets charge by the query, research APIs meter by the call, and paywalled publishers gate content behind payment. When an AI agent encounters one of these resources, the server returns HTTP 402 Payment Required. The agent has no built-in payment mechanism, no budget attached to the session, and no programmatic way to satisfy the request. The task stalls and requires manual intervention. Anchor Browser with Agentic Payments handles machine-to-machine payment workflows on behalf of the agent. Developed in collaboration with the AWS Generative AI Innovation Center Partner Agent Factory , it’s now available on AWS Marketplace . This post covers how Anchor Browser integrates with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments so that AI agents can pay for x402-protected pages and APIs autonomously. The x402 protocol is an open standard for HTTP-based machine-to-machine payments. A server responds with 402 Payment Required along with the amount, accepted payment methods, and payment address that the agent uses to complete the transaction. Anchor Browser is a cloud-based browser automation solution purpose-built for AI agents. Each agent session runs inside a managed browser environment that maintains authentication state, handles navigation, captures network requests, and provides a live view of page interactions. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides capabilities to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore payments is a fully managed capability within AgentCore that AI agents can use to discover, access, and pay for APIs, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, and web content autonomously. AgentCore payments manages wallet connectivity, enforces configurable spending limits at the infrastructure layer, and processes payments through the x402 protocol. It also provides observability into payment attempts, approvals, denials, and settlements through Amazon CloudWatch. When an agent running in Anchor Browser encounters a 402 response, AgentCore payments authorizes and completes the transaction within the configured budget. The workflow continues without interruption. When an autonomous agent encounters an x402-protected resource, the workflow stalls. The agent makes a request, such as fetching a premium research report or calling a paid data enrichment API, and the server responds with HTTP 402 Payment Required. Without a mechanism to pay, the task that was supposed to run autonomously now requires human intervention. Today, developers must build the entire payment stack. This effort spans four categories of complexity: Without a managed payment service, the agent must internalize the entire payment stack. On every x402-protected call that returns a 402 response, the agent must orchestrate the full payment flow internally, including: Each of these steps requires custom code that developers must build, secure, and maintain. Figure 1 illustrates this architecture. The agent contains eight tightly coupled components (Wallet, Private Keys, Budget Controls, Sign Proof, Attach Header, Retry Logic, Settle Payment, and Logging). The agent connects to an x402 API with a 402 challenge flowing back and a retry flowing forward. The security considerations extend beyond the engineering effort. Uncontrolled spending. Without hard spending limits enforced at the infrastructure level, a bug, retry loop, prompt injection, or inadvertent access can trigger unintended payments. An agent retrying a paid endpoint in a loop continues to authorize payments until manual intervention occurs. Key exposure. When private keys reside inside the agent runtime, they share an execution environment with untrusted web pages, third-party tools, and external dependencies. These vectors might inadvertently disclose the credentials that control real funds. Signing flow exposure. If the signing infrastructure is accessible from the runtime, a threat actor can attempt to access the key or redirect payments to an address under unauthorized control. Effective mitigation requires that the key doesn’t enter the runtime in the first place. Browser-based agents introduce an additional constraint: the payment must occur within the same browser session. Otherwise, session recordings and live view no longer match what actually executed. Anchor Browser and AgentCore payments address this complexity by moving the entire payment stack into managed infrastructure. Unlike a stateless tool call, Anchor Browser provides a real cloud browser with persistent identity, repeatable and deterministic workflows, and the session context needed to log in, navigate, and finish tasks reliably. Authentication, navigation, network requests, recordings, and live view happen inside the same browser session. When a payment is required, the transaction happens within that session. The recording captures the full sequence from request to 402 to payment to content delivery. Anchor agents include a built-in x402 tool that handles paid API calls natively within the browser context. The built-in tool requires no changes to existing Playwright, Puppeteer, or Chrome DevTools Protocol-based workflows. AgentCore payments serves as the payment layer. At the center of the service is the Payment Manager, the top-level resource that coordinates payment operations for the AWS account. Creating a Payment Manager requires specifying an authorizer type and an IAM role. AgentCore then provisions a corresponding workload identity in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity. The remaining components connect the Payment Manager to external wallet infrastructure: Anchor Browser sets up wallets through AgentCore payments using a supported wallet provider, without placing wallet secrets or private keys inside the agent runtime. AgentCore payments handles wallet operations through the configured provider. For endpoint discovery, AgentCore provides a curated Coinbase x402 Bazaar MCP s

sources.title: Generate presentations with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: A financial services team spends significant time each week manually creating client PowerPoint presentations from quarterly reports, compliance documents, and market analyses. Each presentation requires reading hundreds of pages, extracting key data points, structuring slides, and generating supporting visuals. This post walks you through building an AI agent system using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that automates this workflow, completing in under 90 seconds in our internal testing. This approach reduces presentation creation time while grounding content in source documents. The solution deploys a supervisor agent on AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, using the Strands Agents framework to orchestrate document generation and summarization tools. Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (available on Amazon Bedrock) handles content creation, Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2 powers vector search, and Stability AI Stable Image Inpaint (available on Amazon Bedrock) generates slide images. This post includes a public repository with the code assets. The solution deploys a single supervisor agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime that selects between document generation and summarization tools based on user requests. A Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline uses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless for vector storage and semantic search across multimodal content. The solution includes a REST API built with .NET 8 minimal APIs, so you can integrate with existing enterprise applications through standard HTTP calls. AWS Lambda offers serverless compute, including containerized functions for PowerPoint generation. The solution secures the implementation with Amazon Virtual Private Cloud (Amazon VPC) isolation, AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) encryption, and AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) least-privilege access control. This section covers AgentCore runtime, RAG, and content safety guardrails as they apply to this solution. A single AI agent generating documents from large knowledge bases must retrieve content, structure outlines, generate text, create images, and assemble files. Rather than implementing these competing responsibilities in a monolithic function, the solution uses a tool-based architecture where a supervisor agent routes requests to specialized tools. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime provides a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with any framework or model. The agent code runs in an isolated container with session management, built-in identity, and observability. The solution uses the Strands Agents framework (an open source SDK for building AI agents) to implement the supervisor logic. The agent determines whether a request requires document generation, content summarization, or both, then invokes the appropriate tool. You can add new capabilities by defining new tools in the agent code without modifying existing ones. RAG addresses a fundamental challenge in AI systems: delivering accurate, up-to-date information grounded in enterprise data rather than relying solely on the model’s training data. The implementation uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases , which combine vector search with large language models (LLMs) to retrieve relevant context before generating responses. This approach is designed to help reduce hallucinated content by grounding generated documents in source information from the enterprise knowledge base. Note: The Amazon OpenSearch Serverless collection data plane must remain publicly accessible because Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases accesses Amazon OpenSearch Serverless from AWS-managed infrastructure, not through customer VPC endpoints. IAM data access policies protect the collection, and VPC-only access restricts the Amazon OpenSearch Serverless dashboard. Enterprise AI applications require content moderation to meet organizational standards and compliance requirements. Amazon Bedrock Guardrails offers built-in content filtering and safety mechanisms integrated throughout the document generation pipeline. The implementation creates custom guardrails through AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) , configured with specific policies tailored to enterprise document creation. The agent applies guardrails at the model invocation level, providing consistent content safety without requiring manual configuration for each deployment. The following diagram illustrates the agent-based document generation system. Figure 1: Architecture of the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore RAG presentation generation system The data flow begins with user requests arriving through Amazon API Gateway , which routes them to a .NET-based Chat API running on AWS Lambda . The API maintains conversation state in Amazon DynamoDB . It then invokes the supervisor agent hosted on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime. The supervisor agent analyzes the request and selects the appropriate tool. For document generation, it invokes the PPTX Generator Lambda (a containerized Python function). For summarization, the supervisor invokes the Summary Generator Lambda, which queries the knowledge base through the retrieve_and_generate API. The system processes, chunks, and embeds documents stored in Amazon S3 using Amazon Titan Text Embeddings v2. Amazon OpenSearch Serverless indexes the embeddings for fast semantic search. When tools query the knowledge base, Amazon OpenSearch Serverless retrieves relevant chunks, which are then supplied as context to Anthropic Claude Sonnet 4.6 (on Amazon Bedrock) for generating grounded responses. The system stores generated documents in Amazon S3 and returns presigned URLs for secure download. sources.title: Building trust in AI agents: A production-ready evaluation framework with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
sources.text: Every organization racing to deploy AI agents faces the same reckoning: an agent that demos beautifully can quietly degrade in production, and by the time a human notices, the trust is already broken. Where traditional software fails loudly, agents fail softly. They return an answer that looks confident, reads fluently, and is wrong. When that answer drives a real business decision, the cost is not a broken feature. It’s a broken relationship with the user. That’s the quality problem at its core. The challenge is therefore not building agents that work once, but proving they keep working, at scale, across every sub-agent, every workflow, and every release. The teams that win the agent era will be the ones who treat quality not as a final QA step but as the operating system of the agent itself: continuously measured, automatically defended, and improved with every interaction. In this post, we show how we built a continuous quality loop for production-ready agentic solutions at scale using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. The solution uses Amazon Bedrock AgentCore and other AWS services for internal use, so sellers and sales leaders can ask business questions in plain English from Amazon Quick. Behind that single experience, several specialized sub-agents work together: the Performance Insights Agent for territory-scoped revenue and performance, the Customer Insights Agent for customer intelligence, the Data Insights Agent for text-to-SQL over foundational datasets, and direct dashboard access. Answers are scoped to each user’s territory and role-level security. Field teams use these answers to assist in planning account strategy, prepare for customer meetings, so the numbers must be right. The most damaging failure is not a crash. It’s a fluent, confident answer that is quietly wrong. Before launch, when we evaluated the Customer Insights Agent, we found exactly that: Through the different runs, monitoring stayed green. It told us the system had responded, not whether the answer was right. Had these errors shipped uncaught, the field would have paid for them. A seller who repeats an inflated figure can lose credibility with the customer. This is exactly why we caught it before launch. The risk doesn’t end at launch: it grows with every new agent and every change to data, prompts, code, or models. It also grows without any release, because upstream pipelines refresh the data every week. Coordinated releases introduce a related risk: when a data change, a tool change, and a paired prompt update are meant to ship together but land apart, the system runs mismatched until all changes catch up. In one pre-production test, that mismatch window by itself dropped the pass rate from 78 percent to 38 percent. To catch failures like these, before every release and continuously in production, we need a framework that can show whether answers are grounded and correct, and trace each failure back to its root cause in the data, the prompt, or the agent’s code. At AWS, the Sales, Marketing, and Global Services (SMGS) Operations team developed a production multi-agent system serving AWS Field Sales worldwide. It serves two distinct audiences. For field sales teams, it replaces hours of manual data analysis with on-demand, conversational intelligence, helping sellers understand the health of their business, surface risks and opportunities, and take action faster. For leadership, it powers business management cadences including Weekly Business Reviews (WBRs), surfacing the signals that matter across the portfolio without requiring manual report preparation. The same agentic system serves both the seller on the front line and the leader reviewing performance at scale. The agentic system orchestrates a growing portfolio of specialized sub-agents, each owning a distinct capability domain. Among them: the Performance Insights Agent generates natural-language business intelligence narratives from complex sales data, turning raw metrics into actionable seller insights. The Customer Insights Agent assembles a 360-degree view of each customer by synthesizing signals across product usage, support history, contract status, and engagement data, helping sellers understand where a customer is in their journey and what they need next. The Data Insights Agent is a text-to-SQL agent that account teams use to query structured analytics data in plain English without writing a single line of SQL. These three agents are the ones referenced throughout the rest of this post. Coordinating these agents reliably at scale made one thing clear: agentic quality wasn’t an operational concern to manage later. It was the prerequisite for operating. A single degraded sub-agent can silently corrupt every response downstream, and traditional monitoring won’t catch it. That reality made a full lifecycle evaluation framework not optional but necessary. AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, is the connective tissue powering it, alongside Amazon Bedrock Guardrails (safety), Amazon CloudWatch (metrics, alarms, tracing), Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) and Amazon Redshift (evaluation persistence), Amazon Quick (dashboards), and AWS Lambda (custom evaluators). In this post, we share how we tackled the hardest operational challenges in running AI agents at enterprise scale, and how Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Evaluations became the backbone of agent quality. Specifically, we cover: Traditional software is deterministic: the same input produces the same output. Machine learning (ML) models introduced probabilistic outputs, and MLOps emerged to manage their training, versioning, monitoring, and re-training. AI agents add a third layer of operational complexity: autonomous, multi-step reasoning, where the question shifts from “did something break?” to “is the agent making sound decisions across its entire reasoning chain?” Agents inherit the hard problems of both predecessors, and introduce some new ones. stories.title: How to Use MiMo-V2.6 for Computer Vision with Roboflow
stories.summary: Try MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Roboflow Playground for OCR, counting, and visual reasoning, then pair it with RF-DETR in Workflows for defect inspection.

sources.name: Roboflow
sources.title: How to Use MiMo-V2.6 for Computer Vision with Roboflow
sources.text: MiMo-V2.6 Flash does well on OCR, counting, and visual reasoning. You can test it in Roboflow Playground, then add it to a Workflow with the OpenRouter block. Roboflow Playground supports more than 130 vision models across 25 vision tasks, including MiMo-V2.6 Flash. In this article, I use Playground to test MiMo on several image-based tasks, then configure the same model in Roboflow Workflows . MiMo-V2.6 is Xiaomi's multimodal model family. It includes two variants: MiMo-V2.6 Pro and MiMo-V2.6 Flash . Both support text, images, video, and audio. Flash is the efficiency-focused version and is the main model tested in this article. For vision tasks, MiMo works differently from a dedicated detector. A detector is designed to return object classes and locations. MiMo can read visible text, describe image content, answer questions, and understand relationships in a scene. Choose MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Roboflow Playground and select the task you want to run. For an OCR test, select OCR and upload the image. The model processes the image directly and returns the detected text. Playground lets you run the same task with different models and compare their results. The tests below focus on MiMo-V2.6 Flash. For questions that do not fit one of the available options, switch to Open Prompt. This mode lets you upload an image and write your own instruction. I used it for the counting test and the visual reasoning test, where the model needed to answer a specific question about the scene. I started with a simple OCR test using a bottle production image. The labels use large, front-facing text, with the lot code and expiry date clearly visible. MiMo-V2.6 Flash read the label correctly, including LOT 241015 and EXP 2025-10-30. For the second test, I used an industrial carton with smaller text, angled labels, barcodes, and glare on parts of the packaging. The model still captured the main label well. It read P/N: 142-7A305 correctly, along with the serial number and lot number. It also picked up the date, pressure range, output value, and the smaller technical text near the bottom of the label. The side label was partly captured. Its angle and partial view make some of the text unclear to check reliably. For that reason, this OCR test focused on text that could actually be read from the source image. For the next test, I switched to Open Prompt and used the same bottle production image. Prompt: How many bottles are visible on the conveyor? Briefly describe the production scene. MiMo-V2.6 Flash counted seven bottles, which matches the image. It also described the scene as an automated orange juice bottling line and recognized the conveyor setup. The response noticed that one bottle was uncapped while the others had caps. The scene description included one inaccurate assumption. MiMo suggested that the uncapped bottle was still in the capping stage. Since capped bottles appear on both sides of it, the image points more toward a missed capping step. The test showed that MiMo could count the bottles correctly and understand the production scene, though its explanation of the uncapped bottle needed closer checking. For the reasoning test, I kept the same production-line image and changed the question. This time, the prompt asked MiMo to find the bottle that broke the visual pattern in the row: Prompt: Which bottle breaks the visual pattern of the row? Give its position from the left and explain the visible difference. MiMo-V2.6 Flash correctly picked the fourth bottle from the left and identified the missing white cap as the difference. To answer the prompt, the model had to spot the anomaly and match it to a specific position in the row. The response matched what was visible in the image without adding another assumption about the production process. After testing MiMo-V2.6 Flash in Playground, the next step was to try the model in Roboflow Workflows with an inspection task . Playground provides a quick way to test MiMo across the available options and see how it handles different types of visual input. Workflows let the model run as part of a reusable pipeline and connect with other processing steps. For this Workflow test, a more challenging production-line image was used with more bottles and several packaging differences. The Workflow sends the image from the Inputs block to the OpenRouter block , then returns the result through the Outputs block. In the OpenRouter settings, the model is set to xiaomi/mimo-v2.6-flash, and the task type is Open Prompt. The prompt asks MiMo to inspect each bottle for visible packaging defects and flag any issues it finds. After running the Workflow, MiMo returned its inspection through the open_router_output field. MiMo flagged two bottles, correctly identifying the sixth from the left as missing its cap and the eighth as having a damaged label. The next bottle had a crooked cap, but MiMo did not flag it in this full-image run. The next Workflow adds an object detection step before MiMo so each bottle can be checked separately. RF-DETR Nano first detects the bottles in the production image, then a Dynamic Crop block creates one crop for each detection and passes those crops to MiMo-V2.6 Flash for inspection. With the bottles cropped, MiMo receives one bottle at a time. The prompt asks it to check the cap and label, then return the result in the same format for every crop: Status: PASS/FAIL | Cap: correct/missing/crooked/uncertain | Label: normal/wrinkled/torn/peeling/uncertain MiMo correctly flagged the bottle with the missing cap and the bottle with the wrinkled label; both results matched the visible defects in the image. The other bottle crops were returned as passes. The bottle with the crooked cap was still classified as “Cap: correct” after it was cropped. MiMo missed the same defect even with a closer view. sources.title: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models
sources.text: Code-Switching Detection via Language-Selective Dimensions in Speech Foundation Models Authors Jie Chi, Zakaria Aldeneh, Masha Fedzechkina, Maureen de Seyssel, Natalie Schluter Code-switching (CS), the alternation between languages within an utterance, is common in multilingual speech but underrepresented in pretraining corpora. Increasing CS coverage requires finding relevant utterances in large speech collections so that they can be included in training data. One way to find such utterances is to transcribe the speech and detect language alternation in the text, but this depends on obtaining accurate multilingual transcriptions. We propose a lightweight method that detects CS directly from speech. It uses frame-level language information in pretrained speech encoders to determine whether both languages are present within an utterance. Specifically, we identify language-selective hidden-state dimensions using monolingual recordings and aggregate their frame-level activations into a CS prediction. With a small CS set used to tune a decision rule, we show that the Whisper-small encoder achieves a mean F1 of 0.798 across 14 language pairs in CS-FLEURS, compared with 0.776 for a CNN and 0.751 for a HuBERT linear baseline trained for monolingual language identification. Our findings suggest that pretrained speech encoders already encode the information needed to identify CS utterances, and they provide a lightweight tool for building more representative multilingual corpora. sources.title: The Design Space of Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Models
sources.text: The Design Space of Tri-Modal Masked Diffusion Models Authors Louis BÃ©thune, Victor Turrisi, Bruno Kacper Mlodozeniecâ **, Pau Rodriguez Lopez, Lokesh Boominathan, Nikhil Bhendawade, Amitis Shidani, Joris Pelemans, Theo X. Olaussonâ¡**, Devon Hjelm, Paul Dixon, JoÃ£o Monteiro, Pierre Ablin, Vishnu Banna, Arno Blaas, Nick Henderson, Kari Noriy, Dan Busbridge, Josh Susskind, Marco Cuturi, Irina Belousova, Luca Zappella, Russ Webb, Jason RamapuramÂ§** Discrete diffusion models have emerged as strong alternatives to autoregressive language models, with recent work initializing and finetuning a base unimodal model for bi-modal generation. Diverging from previous approaches, we introduce the first tri-modal Masked Diffusion Models (MDM) pretrained from scratch on text, image-text, and audio-text data. We systematically analyze multimodal scaling laws, modality mixing ratios, noise schedules, batch-size effects and provide optimized inference sampling defaults. Our batch-size analysis yields a novel stochastic differential equation (SDE) based reparameterization, eliminating the need for tuning the optimal batch size as reported in recent work. This reparameterization decouples the physical batch size, often chosen based on compute (GPU saturation, FLOP-efficiency, wall-clock time) from the logical batch size, chosen to balance the variance of gradients during stochastic optimization. Finally, we pretrain a preliminary model showcasing the capabilities of a unified design, achieving strong results at 3B model scale (6.4T tokens), in both text generation, T2I tasks, and T2S tasks. Our work represents the largest scale systematic open study of multimodal discrete diffusion models conducted to date, providing valuable insights into scaling behaviors across multiple modalities.
